claim: Delta-Notch signalling regulates cell fate decisions in multiple cell lineages owing to unidirectional signalling between daughter cells.
source: In multiple cell lineages, Delta-Notch signalling regulates cell fate decisions owing to unidirectional signalling between daughter cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about Delta-Notch signaling that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In Drosophila pupal sensory organ lineage, Notch regulates the intra-lineage pIIa/pIIb fate decision at cytokinesis.
source: In Drosophila pupal sensory organ lineage, Notch regulates the intra-lineage pIIa/pIIb fate decision at cytokinesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Notch function in Drosophila sensory organ development.

claim: Notch and Delta localise apically and basally at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: Notch and Delta that localise apically and basally at the pIIa-pIIb interface are expressed at low levels and their residence time at the plasma membrane is in the order of minutes.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior published work and observations in the field.

claim: Notch and Delta are expressed at low levels at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: Notch and Delta that localise apically and basally at the pIIa-pIIb interface are expressed at low levels and their residence time at the plasma membrane is in the order of minutes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and prior observations in the field.

claim: The residence time of Notch and Delta at the plasma membrane is in the order of minutes.
source: Notch and Delta that localise apically and basally at the pIIa-pIIb interface are expressed at low levels and their residence time at the plasma membrane is in the order of minutes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: The signalling interface possesses a unique apico-basal polarity with Par3/Bazooka localising in the form of nano-clusters at the apical and basal level.
source: Here, we report that the signalling interface possesses a unique apico-basal polarity with Par3/Bazooka localising in the form of nano-clusters at the apical and basal level.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the manuscript based on experimental observations.

claim: Notch is preferentially targeted to the pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: Notch is preferentially targeted to the pIIa-pIIb interface, where it co-clusters with Bazooka and its cofactor Sanpodo.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Notch co-clusters with Bazooka and Sanpodo at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: Notch is preferentially targeted to the pIIa-pIIb interface, where it co-clusters with Bazooka and its cofactor Sanpodo.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental observations and imaging data.

claim: Cluster assembly relies on Bazooka and Sanpodo activities.
source: Clusters whose assembly relies on Bazooka and Sanpodo activities are also positive for Neuralized, the E3 ligase required for Delta activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on genetic and functional experiments in the manuscript.

claim: Clusters are positive for Neuralized, the E3 ligase required for Delta activity.
source: Clusters whose assembly relies on Bazooka and Sanpodo activities are also positive for Neuralized, the E3 ligase required for Delta activity.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations showing Neuralized localization in clusters.

claim: The nano-clusters act as snap buttons at the new pIIa-pIIb interface to allow efficient intra-lineage signalling.
source: We propose that the nano-clusters act as snap buttons at the new pIIa-pIIb interface to allow efficient intra-lineage signalling.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings and interpretations in the manuscript.

claim: Notch is the receptor of an evolutionarily conserved cell-cell signalling pathway that controls fate acquisition in numerous processes throughout metazoan development.
source: Notch is the receptor of an evolutionarily conserved cell-cell signalling pathway that controls fate acquisition in numerous processes throughout metazoan development (Kopan and Ilagan, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Within many cell lineages, following the division of a precursor cell, Notch activation regulates binary fate choice between daughter cells.
source: Within many cell lineages, following the division of a precursor cell, Notch activation regulates binary fate choice between daughter cells (Bertet et al., 2014; Bivik et al., 2016; Dong et al., 2012; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007; Pardo-Saganta et al., 2015; San-Juan and Baonza, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: In the majority of cases, the Notch receptor is activated by transmembrane ligands present in the adjacent cell.
source: In the majority of cases, the Notch receptor is activated by transmembrane ligands present in the adjacent cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Notch signaling mechanisms.

claim: Following binding to Notch, endocytosis of the ligand generates pulling forces, driving a change in the conformation of the Notch extracellular domain, leading to the exposure of the S2 cleavage site of Notch.
source: Following binding to Notch, endocytosis of the ligand generates pulling forces, driving a change in the conformation of the Notch extracellular domain, leading to the exposure of the S2 cleavage site of Notch (Gordon et al., 2015; Langridge and Struhl, 2017; Meloty-Kapella et al., 2012; Seo et al., 2016; Shergill et al., 2012; Wang and Ha, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: The mechanosensitive cleavage of Notch is followed by a constitutive proteolytic cleavage by the gamma secretase complex.
source: This mechanosensitive cleavage is followed by a constitutive proteolytic cleavage of Notch by the gamma secretase complex (Mumm et al., 2000; Struhl and Adachi, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage of Notch gives rise to the transcriptionally active Notch intracellular domain (NICD).
source: This gives rise to the transcriptionally active Notch intracellular domain (NICD) (Kopan and Ilagan, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Proteolytic activation of the Notch receptor is irreversible.
source: Since proteolytic activation of the Notch receptor is irreversible, Notch activation needs to be tightly controlled in time and in space.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Notch signaling.

claim: Sensory organ precursors (SOPs) of the pupal notum of Drosophila have been instrumental in the study of intra-lineage, Notch-dependent fate decisions.
source: Sensory organ precursors (SOPs) of the pupal notum of Drosophila have been instrumental in the study of intra-lineage, Notch-dependent fate decisions (Schweisguth, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: SOPs are epithelial cells that divide asymmetrically within the plane of a single-layer epithelium to generate two daughter cells, an anterior pIIb cell and a posterior pIIa cell.
source: SOPs are epithelial cells that divide asymmetrically within the plane of a single-layer epithelium to generate two daughter cells, an anterior pIIb cell and a posterior pIIa cell, which are precursors of internal and external cells of the sensory organ, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SOP cell division.

claim: The pIIa-pIIb fate acquisition relies on the differential activation of Notch during cytokinesis as a result of the unequal partitioning of Numb and Neuralized (Neur) in the pIIb cell.
source: The pIIa-pIIb fate acquisition relies on the differential activation of Notch during cytokinesis as a result of the unequal partitioning of Numb and Neuralized (Neur) in the pIIb cell (Le Borgne and Schweisguth, 2003; Rhyu et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In pIIb, Numb interacts with and regulates the trafficking of Sanpodo (Spdo), a four-pass transmembrane protein interacting with Notch and required for Notch signalling.
source: In pIIb, Numb interacts with and regulates the trafficking of Sanpodo (Spdo), a four-pass transmembrane protein interacting with Notch and required for Notch signalling (Babaoglan et al., 2009; Cotton et al., 2013; Couturier et al., 2013; O'Connor-Giles and Skeath, 2003, Johnson et al., 2016; Upadhyay et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Numb causes the targeting of Spdo/Notch to late endosomes.
source: Numb causes the targeting of Spdo/Notch to late endosomes (Cotton et al., 2013; Couturier et al., 2013), whereas Neur promotes the endocytosis of the Notch ligand Delta (Dl) (Le Borgne and Schweisguth, 2003), so that Notch is inhibited in pIIb and activated in pIIa.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Neur promotes the endocytosis of the Notch ligand Delta (Dl).
source: Numb causes the targeting of Spdo/Notch to late endosomes (Cotton et al., 2013; Couturier et al., 2013), whereas Neur promotes the endocytosis of the Notch ligand Delta (Dl) (Le Borgne and Schweisguth, 2003), so that Notch is inhibited in pIIb and activated in pIIa.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Notch is inhibited in pIIb and activated in pIIa.
source: Numb causes the targeting of Spdo/Notch to late endosomes (Cotton et al., 2013; Couturier et al., 2013), whereas Neur promotes the endocytosis of the Notch ligand Delta (Dl) (Le Borgne and Schweisguth, 2003), so that Notch is inhibited in pIIb and activated in pIIa.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited mechanisms of Numb and Neur function.

claim: During SOP cytokinesis, two pools of Notch, located apically and basally to the midbody, are present at the pIIb-pIIa interface and both contribute to Notch signalling.
source: During SOP cytokinesis, two pools of Notch, located apically and basally to the midbody, are present at the pIIb-pIIa interface and both contribute to Notch signalling (Bellec et al., 2021; Trylinski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The basal pool of Notch is the main contributor of NICD.
source: Previous studies based on photobleaching and photoconversion experiments have revealed that the basal pool of Notch is the main contributor of NICD (Trylinski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In vertebrates, the scaffolding protein Par3 regulates Numb-mediated trafficking of integrin and amyloid precursor protein (APP).
source: In vertebrates, the scaffolding protein Par3 regulates Numb-mediated trafficking of integrin and amyloid precursor protein (APP).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Par3 function in vertebrates.

claim: By binding to the phosphotyrosine domain of Numb, Par3 precludes Numb from binding to integrin, thus hindering Numb from causing integrin endocytosis.
source: Indeed, by binding to the phosphotyrosine domain of Numb, Par3 precludes Numb from binding to integrin, thus hindering Numb from causing integrin endocytosis (Nishimura and Kaibuchi, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Par3 interferes with the interaction between Numb and APP.
source: Similarly, Par3 interferes with the interaction between Numb and APP.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Par3 function.

claim: In the absence of Par3, there is an increase in Numb-APP interaction leading to decreased surface APP and increased targeting of APP to late endosomal-lysosomal compartments.
source: In the absence of Par3, there is an increase in Numb-APP interaction leading to decreased surface APP and increased targeting of APP to late endosomal-lysosomal compartments (Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Par3 regulates adherens junction (AJs) organisation and forms a complex with Par6 and atypical protein kinase C (aPKC).
source: In addition to regulating Numb-mediated membrane trafficking, Par3 regulates adherens junction (AJs) organisation and forms a complex with Par6 and atypical protein kinase C (aPKC), a complex that is essential in the establishment or maintenance of epithelial cell apico-basal polarity (Assemat et al., 2008; Goldstein and Macara, 2007; Laprise and Tepass, 2011; Nelson, 2003; Rodriguez-Boulan and Macara, 2014; St Johnston and Ahringer, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The Par3/Par6/aPKC complex is essential in the establishment or maintenance of epithelial cell apico-basal polarity.
source: In addition to regulating Numb-mediated membrane trafficking, Par3 regulates adherens junction (AJs) organisation and forms a complex with Par6 and atypical protein kinase C (aPKC), a complex that is essential in the establishment or maintenance of epithelial cell apico-basal polarity (Assemat et al., 2008; Goldstein and Macara, 2007; Laprise and Tepass, 2011; Nelson, 2003; Rodriguez-Boulan and Macara, 2014; St Johnston and Ahringer, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: During SOP mitosis, the unequal segregation of Numb relies on the SOP-specific remodelling of polarity modules and the phosphorylation by the Baz-aPKC-Par6 complex.
source: During SOP mitosis, the unequal segregation of Numb relies on the SOP-specific remodelling of polarity modules and the phosphorylation by the Baz-aPKC-Par6 complex (Bellaïche et al., 2001; Wirtz-Peitz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Prior to mitotic entry, aPKC-Par6 are in complex with the tumour suppressor lethal giant larvae (Lgl).
source: Prior to mitotic entry, aPKC-Par6 are in complex with the tumour suppressor lethal giant larvae (Lgl).
evidence: This is established knowledge about polarity complex dynamics during mitosis.

claim: Assembly of the Baz-aPKC-Par6 complex is initiated upon phosphorylation of Par6 by the mitotic kinase AuroraA (AurA).
source: Assembly of the Baz-aPKC-Par6 complex is initiated upon phosphorylation of Par6 by the mitotic kinase AuroraA (AurA), then causing the autoactivation of aPKC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about polarity complex assembly.

claim: Phosphorylation of Par6 by AuroraA causes the autoactivation of aPKC.
source: Assembly of the Baz-aPKC-Par6 complex is initiated upon phosphorylation of Par6 by the mitotic kinase AuroraA (AurA), then causing the autoactivation of aPKC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about polarity complex activation.

claim: aPKC triggers the phosphorylation of Lgl.
source: aPKC next triggers the phosphorylation of Lgl.
evidence: This is established knowledge about aPKC function.

claim: Phosphorylated aPKC and Par6 can assemble with Baz.
source: Phosphorylated aPKC and Par6 can assemble with Baz (Wirtz-Peitz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The Baz complex localises at the posterior apical and lateral cortex during SOP mitosis.
source: The Baz complex localises at the posterior apical and lateral cortex, while discs-large (Dlg) and partner of inscuteable (Pins) accumulate at the anterior lateral cortex during SOP mitosis (Bellaïche et al., 2001; Roegiers et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Dlg and Pins accumulate at the anterior lateral cortex during SOP mitosis.
source: The Baz complex localises at the posterior apical and lateral cortex, while discs-large (Dlg) and partner of inscuteable (Pins) accumulate at the anterior lateral cortex during SOP mitosis (Bellaïche et al., 2001; Roegiers et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Baz complex phosphorylates Numb at the posterior cortex, thereby preventing Numb to localise there, resulting in the unequal distribution of Numb in the anterior cortex.
source: Baz complex phosphorylates Numb at the posterior cortex, thereby preventing Numb to localise there, resulting in the unequal distribution of Numb in the anterior cortex (Smith et al., 2007; Wirtz-Peitz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Following degradation of AurA at metaphase to anaphase transition, Baz may be released from the Par6-aPKC complex.
source: Following degradation of AurA at metaphase to anaphase transition, Baz may be released from the Par6-aPKC complex.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from known mechanisms.

claim: Crb-GFP is detected faster at the new apical pIIa-pIIb interface than between epidermal daughters.
source: Crb-GFP is detected faster at the new apical pIIa-pIIb interface than between epidermal daughters (Figure 1A–A'', Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: In pIIa and pIIb cells, Crb-GFP localises primarily in apical cytoplasmic puncta at the expense of the pIIa-pIIb cell interface.
source: Then, while Crb remains localised at the apical interface of epidermal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–C'), in pIIa and pIIb cells Crb-GFP localises primarily in apical cytoplasmic puncta (t13 ±4 min; Figure 1A–A'' and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C'), at the expense of the pIIa-pIIb cell interface (t23 ±4 min).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in the figures.

claim: aPKC-GFP is first localised at the new pIIa-pIIb interface and then redistributed in part to cytoplasmic puncta primarily in the pIIa cell.
source: A similar behaviour was observed for aPKC-GFP, which is first localised at the new pIIa-pIIb interface (t7 ± 1 min; Figure 1B–B'', and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E) and then redistributed in part to cytoplasmic puncta primarily in the pIIa cell.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in the figures.

claim: Baz-GFP is not relocalised in apical cytoplasmic puncta in contrast to aPKC and Crb.
source: In striking contrast to aPKC and Crb, Baz-GFP is not relocalised in apical cytoplasmic puncta.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations comparing Baz localization to aPKC and Crb.

claim: Baz-GFP is localised both at the pIIa-pIIb interface and is enriched at the posterior pole of the pIIa cell.
source: Instead, Baz-GFP is localised both at the pIIa-pIIb interface and is also enriched at the posterior pole of the pIIa cell (Figure 1C–C'' and t9 min), in agreement with previous reports (Le Borgne et al., 2002; Roegiers et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and is consistent with prior published reports.

claim: Baz-GFP is localised in punctate structures at the lateral pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: Finally, Baz-GFP is localised in punctate structures at the lateral pIIa-pIIb interface (Figure 1C–C" middle panels and orthogonal views, see also Video 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in the figures and video.

claim: Lateral interface clusters of Baz are specific to the interface of SOP daughter cells.
source: These punctate structures, which we will refer to as lateral interface clusters and are specific to the interface of SOP daughter cells, appear at the same time as the first apical Baz clusters, ~ 10 min after the onset of anaphase (Figure 1C–C'').
evidence: This is based on experimental observations comparing SOP and epidermal cell interfaces.

claim: Lateral interface clusters appear approximately 10 min after the onset of anaphase.
source: These punctate structures, which we will refer to as lateral interface clusters and are specific to the interface of SOP daughter cells, appear at the same time as the first apical Baz clusters, ~ 10 min after the onset of anaphase (Figure 1C–C'').
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging data.

claim: When an SOP expressing NiGFP is dividing next to epidermal cells expressing untagged Notch, the NiGFP signal is detected at the apical pIIa-pIIb interface, and basally between the pIIa-pIIb nuclei.
source: When an SOP expressing NiGFP is dividing next to epidermal cells expressing untagged Notch (Figure 2A), the NiGFP signal is detected at the apical pIIa-pIIb interface, and basally between the pIIa-pIIb nuclei (Figure 2A' and t21).
evidence: This is based on clone border analysis experiments shown in the figures.

claim: When a SOP expressing untagged Notch is dividing next to epidermal cells expressing NiGFP, no GFP signal is detected at the apical and basal pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: In the converse situation, when a SOP expressing untagged Notch is dividing next to epidermal cells expressing NiGFP, no GFP signal is detected at the apical and basal pIIa-pIIb interface (Figure 2B–B').
evidence: This is based on clone border analysis experiments shown in the figures.

claim: Low NiGFP signal is detected at the boundary between pIIa or pIIb and their neighbouring epidermal cells.
source: Analyses of clone boundaries also reveal that low NiGFP signal is detected at the boundary between pIIa or pIIb and their neighbouring epidermal cells.
evidence: This is based on clone border analysis experiments.

claim: In epidermal cells, Notch equally partitions along the plasma membrane.
source: This is not observed in epidermal cells where Notch equally partitions along the plasma membrane (Figure 2A' and B', and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in the figures.

claim: Following SOP division, Notch is preferentially transported towards or stabilised at the pIIa-pIIb interface where signalling takes place.
source: These data show that, following SOP division, Notch is preferentially transported towards or stabilised at the pIIa-pIIb interface where signalling takes place.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clone border analysis data.

claim: Ubi-Baz-mCherry colocalises with NiGFP in punctae along the pIIa-pIIb apical interface as well as in lateral interface clusters.
source: We first observed that Ubi-Baz-mCherry colocalises with NiGFP in punctae along the pIIa-pIIb apical interface as well as in lateral interface clusters (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on co-imaging experiments shown in the figure.

claim: The NiGFP/Baz lateral interface clusters do not correspond to spot AJs (SAJs).
source: The NiGFP/Baz lateral interface clusters do not correspond to spot AJs (SAJs) (McGill et al., 2009), as E-Cad and Baz do not colocalise at the lateral pIIa-pIIb interface (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations showing lack of colocalization with E-Cad.

claim: At the apical pIIa-pIIb interface and lateral interface, the Ubi-Baz-mCherry and NiGFP tracks colocalise to a greater extent compared with the epidermal-epidermal interface.
source: Kymographs of these acquisitions (Figure 2E and E') show that, at the apical pIIa-pIIb interface and even more markedly at the lateral interface, the Ubi-Baz-mCherry and NiGFP tracks colocalise to a greater extent compared with the epidermal-epidermal interface (Figure 2E–E'').
evidence: This is based on kymograph analysis of high spatio-temporal resolution imaging data.

claim: Notch is dispensable for assembly of Baz clusters.
source: Under these conditions, Baz still localises in clusters along the apico-basal pIIa-pIIb interface as in the wild type, indicating that Notch is dispensable for assembly of Baz clusters (Figure 3E–F', yellow arrowheads).
evidence: This is based on experiments depleting Notch and observing Baz localization.

claim: Upon Baz silencing, the fluorescence intensity of the apical NiGFP clusters as well as the number and intensity of the lateral interface clusters decrease.
source: Upon Baz silencing, the fluorescence intensity of the apical NiGFP clusters as well as the number and intensity of the lateral interface clusters decrease (Figure 4A–B' and E–E' and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is based on RNAi experiments and quantification shown in the figures.

claim: A similar decrease in Notch clusters was observed in bazEH747 clones, a genetic and protein null allele of Baz.
source: A similar decrease was observed in bazEH747 clones, a genetic and protein null allele of Baz (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D'; Shahab et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on genetic mutant analysis shown in the figures.

claim: The decrease of apical and lateral interface cluster number and fluorescence intensity is accompanied by a partial defect of Notch activation upon silencing of Baz.
source: Interestingly, the decrease of apical and lateral interface cluster number and fluorescence intensity is accompanied by a partial defect of Notch activation upon silencing of Baz (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B'), as well as in bazEH747 homozygous mutant SO (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, E').
evidence: This is based on lineage analysis experiments shown in the figures.

claim: Baz, while not completely essential, is required for proper activation of Notch signalling in the pIIa cell.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that Baz, while not completely essential, is required for proper activation of Notch signalling in the pIIa cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing partial Notch activation defects.

claim: A higher number of and brighter lateral interface clusters of NiGFP, accompanied with an increased transient NiGFP apical level, were observed upon silencing of Delta.
source: A higher number of and brighter lateral interface clusters of NiGFP, accompanied with an increased transient NiGFP apical level, were observed upon silencing of Delta (Figure 4A, A', C–C", E and E').
evidence: This is based on RNAi experiments and quantification shown in the figures.

claim: Concomitant silencing of Baz and Delta leads to a strong neurogenic phenotype resulting in a penetrant loss of Notch function.
source: We found that their concomitant silencing leads to a strong neurogenic phenotype resulting a bald cuticle, that is, a penetrant loss of Notch function (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, A' and D, D').
evidence: This is based on double RNAi experiments and phenotypic analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Upon simultaneous silencing of Baz and Delta, NiGFP was no longer stabilised in clusters at the apical or lateral interface.
source: Strikingly, under this experimental situation, NiGFP was no longer stabilised in clusters at the apical or lateral interface (Figure 4D–E'), indicating that both Delta and Baz cooperate to stabilise Notch clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
evidence: This is based on double RNAi experiments shown in the figures.

claim: Both Delta and Baz cooperate to stabilise Notch clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: Strikingly, under this experimental situation, NiGFP was no longer stabilised in clusters at the apical or lateral interface (Figure 4D–E'), indicating that both Delta and Baz cooperate to stabilise Notch clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results from double RNAi.

claim: Neur-GFP localises asymmetrically at the anterior cortex, opposite to Baz during SOP prometaphase, and is unequally partitioned in pIIb cell.
source: As previously reported, Neur-GFP (Perez-Mockus et al., 2017) localises asymmetrically at the anterior cortex, opposite to Baz during SOP prometaphase, and is unequally partitioned in pIIb cell (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations consistent with prior reports.

claim: At t21 min, Neur is localised in clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface where it largely colocalises with Baz-Scarlet.
source: At t21 min, Neur is localised in clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface where it largely colocalises with Baz-Scarlet (Figure 5A and insets).
evidence: This is based on co-imaging experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Loss of Neur results in a Notch loss-of-function phenotype.
source: Loss of Neur results in a Notch loss-of-function phenotype (Lai and Rubin, 2001) and an increased transient signal of NiGFP at the apical pIIb-pIIb-like interface (Figure 5B–C) accompanied with a higher number and brighter lateral interface clusters of NiGFP (Figure 5B, B', C' and C"), which persists for more than 36 min after anaphase onset.
evidence: This is based on genetic mutant analysis and is consistent with prior reports.

claim: Loss of Neur results in an increased transient signal of NiGFP at the apical pIIb-pIIb-like interface accompanied with a higher number and brighter lateral interface clusters of NiGFP.
source: Loss of Neur results in a Notch loss-of-function phenotype (Lai and Rubin, 2001) and an increased transient signal of NiGFP at the apical pIIb-pIIb-like interface (Figure 5B–C) accompanied with a higher number and brighter lateral interface clusters of NiGFP (Figure 5B, B', C' and C"), which persists for more than 36 min after anaphase onset.
evidence: This is based on genetic mutant analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Upon loss of Neur, Baz still localises at the apical interface and in lateral interface clusters, but the number of Baz-positive lateral cluster is significantly increased.
source: While upon loss of Neur, Baz still localises at the apical interface and in lateral interface clusters, the number of Baz-positive lateral cluster is significantly increased upon silencing of Neur (Figure 5D–D").
evidence: This is based on experiments analyzing Baz localization in Neur mutants.

claim: Baz and NiGFP remain closely associated at the apical and lateral interface clusters upon loss of Neur.
source: Analyses of their dynamics at high spatio-temporal resolution revealed that Baz and NiGFP remain closely associated at the apical and lateral interface clusters upon loss of Neur (Figure 5E and E').
evidence: This is based on high-resolution imaging analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Neur, Delta, Baz, and Notch localise in apical and lateral interface clusters and their numbers and signal intensities depend on Neur and Delta activity, on the one hand, and on Baz activity, on the other hand.
source: Collectively, these results argue that Neur, Delta, Baz, and Notch localise in apical and lateral interface clusters and that their numbers and signal intensities depend on Neur and Delta activity, on the one hand, and on Baz activity, on the other hand.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective experimental results.

claim: Clusters are assembled but fail to be disassembled in a timely manner upon Neur silencing.
source: These data further suggest that clusters are assembled but fail to be disassembled in a timely manner upon Neur silencing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of persistent clusters in Neur mutants.

claim: Numb does not colocalise with Baz-Scarlet-positive clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: In contrast to Neur, Numb does not colocalise with Baz-Scarlet-positive clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on co-imaging experiments shown in the figure.

claim: The accumulation of lateral Notch clusters persists until at least 36 min after anaphase onset upon silencing of Numb.
source: These data are consistent with those previously published (Couturier et al., 2012; Trylinski et al., 2017), and further show that the accumulation of lateral Notch clusters persists until at least 36 min after anaphase onset.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and is consistent with prior reports.

claim: Upon silencing of Numb, Baz localises in lateral interface clusters at the pIIa-pIIa like interface where it colocalises with NiGFP.
source: Upon silencing of Numb, Baz localises in lateral interface clusters at the pIIa-pIIa like interface (Figure 6D, D' and E), where it colocalises with NiGFP, as revealed by the dynamics of the Baz-Notch clusters at high spatio-temporal resolution (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on RNAi experiments and high-resolution imaging shown in the figures.

claim: Numb decreases the number of Notch-Baz clusters.
source: Together, these data indicate that Numb decreases the number of Notch-Baz clusters.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing increased clusters upon Numb depletion.

claim: Notch-Baz clusters are assembled in the anterior cell upon loss of Numb and contribute to Notch activation in this cell.
source: As Numb is present and regulates Notch endosomal trafficking in the anterior pIIb cell (Cotton et al., 2013; Couturier et al., 2013), our data suggest that Notch-Baz clusters are assembled in the anterior cell upon loss of Numb and contribute to Notch activation in this cell.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and prior knowledge about Numb function.

claim: Numb acts antagonistically to Baz to promote Notch clusters assembly and/or stability.
source: This model further suggests that Numb acts antagonistically to Baz to promote Notch clusters assembly and/or stability.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Upon overexpression of Numb, NiGFP is no longer detected along the pIIb-pIIb-like interface, either apically or laterally.
source: To test this prediction, we overexpressed Numb in the SOP and daughter cells and observed that NiGFP is no longer detected along the pIIb-pIIb-like interface, either apically or laterally (Figure 6D'').
evidence: This is based on overexpression experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Upon Numb overexpression, while Baz localises uniformly at the apical SOP daughter cell interface, lateral interface clusters are barely detectable.
source: While Baz localises uniformly at the apical SOP daughter cell interface, lateral interface clusters are barely detectable (t14, Figure 6D'', bottom panels, and E).
evidence: This is based on overexpression experiments shown in the figures.

claim: Numb and Baz act antagonistically, as has been proposed in vertebrates.
source: These data raise the possibility that Numb and Baz act antagonistically, as has been proposed in vertebrates (Nishimura and Kaibuchi, 2007; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and comparison to vertebrate studies.

claim: Baz-Scarlet and Spdo-GFP colocalise both at the apical pIIa-pIIb interface and in lateral clusters.
source: On live specimens, Baz-Scarlet and Spdo-GFP (Couturier et al., 2013) colocalise both at the apical pIIa-pIIb interface and in lateral clusters (Figure 7A, t21).
evidence: This is based on co-imaging experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Baz-positive lateral clusters are no longer detectable upon loss of Spdo.
source: Compared with the control situation, Baz-positive lateral clusters are no longer detectable upon loss of Spdo (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on genetic mutant analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Loss of Spdo results in an increase of NiGFP signal at the apical interface of SOP daughters and the appearance of a continuous and nebulous staining of NiGFP instead of the characteristic, well-defined, lateral clusters.
source: In agreement with the findings of Couturier et al., 2012, loss of Spdo also results in an increase of NiGFP signal at the apical interface of SOP daughters and the appearance of a continuous and nebulous staining of NiGFP instead of the characteristic, well-defined, lateral clusters observed at the pIIa-pIIb interface of controls SO (Figure 7C and D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-A',C-C').
evidence: This is based on genetic mutant analysis and is consistent with prior reports.

claim: NiGFP persists at the apical interface compared with the control upon loss of Spdo, and NiGFP is detected apically, in the cytoplasm or at the apical plasma membrane, indicative of higher levels of Notch.
source: We also noticed that NiGFP persists at the apical interface compared with the control, and that NiGFP is detected apically, in the cytoplasm or at the apical plasma membrane, indicative of higher levels of Notch upon loss of Spdo (Figure 7C,D,t15 and t30, upper panels).
evidence: This is based on observations from genetic mutant analysis shown in the figures.

claim: FRAP analyses revealed that the NiGFP signal at the apical interface is recovered 1.9 times faster, with a mobile fraction 1.6 times higher than in the control situation upon loss of Spdo.
source: Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) analyses revealed that the NiGFP signal at the apical interface is recovered 1.9 times faster, with a mobile fraction 1.6 times higher than in the control situation (Figure 7E and E' and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on FRAP experiments shown in the figures.

claim: The changes in NiGFP distribution and time residence at the pIIb-pIIb-like interface are accompanied by a loss of colocalisation of NiGFP and Baz-mCherry at the apical and lateral pIIb-pIIb-like interface upon Spdo silencing.
source: The changes in NiGFP distribution and time residence at the pIIb-pIIb-like interface are accompanied by a loss of colocalisation of NiGFP and Baz-mCherry at the apical and lateral pIIb-pIIb-like interface upon Spdo silencing (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D').
evidence: This is based on RNAi experiments and colocalization analysis shown in the figures.

claim: Spdo co-clusters with Baz and Notch at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: We first concluded that Spdo co-clusters with Baz and Notch at the pIIa-pIIb interface and, second, that the activity of Spdo is required for the clustering of Baz/Notch along the pIIa-pIIb interface to promote Notch activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the colocalization and functional experiments.

claim: The activity of Spdo is required for the clustering of Baz/Notch along the pIIa-pIIb interface to promote Notch activation.
source: We first concluded that Spdo co-clusters with Baz and Notch at the pIIa-pIIb interface and, second, that the activity of Spdo is required for the clustering of Baz/Notch along the pIIa-pIIb interface to promote Notch activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional experiments showing loss of clusters upon Spdo depletion.

claim: Baz, but not aPKC, co-partitions with Notch, Spdo, and Neur in apical and lateral clusters.
source: In this study, we have characterised the remodelling of apico-basal cell polarity occurring during SOP division leading to a specific pIIa-pIIb Notch signalling interface. We report that Baz, but not aPKC, co-partitions with Notch, Spdo, and Neur in apical and lateral clusters.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings from the study.

claim: The assembly of Notch/Baz/Spdo/Neur clusters requires Baz and Spdo activities.
source: The assembly of these clusters requires Baz and Spdo activities, and their number and dynamics are regulated by Delta, Neur and Numb activities.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings from the study.

claim: The number and dynamics of Notch/Baz/Spdo/Neur clusters are regulated by Delta, Neur and Numb activities.
source: The assembly of these clusters requires Baz and Spdo activities, and their number and dynamics are regulated by Delta, Neur and Numb activities.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings from the study.

claim: In the absence of Numb, the number of clusters increases.
source: In the absence of Numb, the number of clusters increases, while overexpression of Numb results in their disappearance, suggesting that Numb and Baz act antagonistically.
evidence: This is based on experimental results from Numb depletion and overexpression.

claim: Overexpression of Numb results in the disappearance of clusters.
source: In the absence of Numb, the number of clusters increases, while overexpression of Numb results in their disappearance, suggesting that Numb and Baz act antagonistically.
evidence: This is based on experimental results from Numb overexpression.

claim: Notch/Baz/Spdo/Neur clusters represent the Notch signalling units at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: We propose a model according to which Notch/Baz/Spdo/Neur clusters represent the Notch signalling units at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: During SOP cytokinesis coinciding with the presumptive proteolytic degradation of AurA, the Baz/Par6/aPKC complex disassembles with aPKC redistributing like Crb in apical intracellular compartments.
source: Here, we report that during cytokinesis coinciding with the presumptive proteolytic degradation of AurA, the Baz /Par6/aPKC complex disassembles with aPKC redistributing like Crb in apical intracellular compartments.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental observations.

claim: Baz redistributes apically at the posterior pole of the pIIa cell and in the form of clusters at the apical and lateral pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: In contrast to aPKC, Baz redistributes apically at the posterior pole of the pIIa cell and in the form of clusters at the apical and lateral pIIa-pIIb interface.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental observations.

claim: Lateral clusters of Baz are only found at the pIIa-pIIb interface, indicating that the SOP-specific remodelling polarity that takes place at SOP mitosis is instrumental in formation of clusters.
source: Such lateral clusters of Baz are only found at the pIIa-pIIb interface, indicating that the SOP-specific remodelling polarity that takes place at SOP mitosis is instrumental in formation of clusters.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that lateral clusters are specific to SOP daughters.

claim: Baz has been reported to be excluded from the lateral plasma membrane following Par1-mediated phosphorylation.
source: Baz has been reported to be excluded from the lateral plasma membrane following Par1-mediated phosphorylation (Benton and St Johnston, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Phosphorylation of Baz by Par1 activity is antagonised by type 2 A protein phosphatase (PP2A) activity.
source: In addition, phosphorylation of Baz by Par1 activity is antagonised by type 2 A protein phosphatase (PP2A) activity (Krahn et al., 2009), and silencing of tws, the regulatory B subunit of PP2A, results in Notch gain-of-function phenotype (Shiomi et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Silencing of tws, the regulatory B subunit of PP2A, results in Notch gain-of-function phenotype.
source: In addition, phosphorylation of Baz by Par1 activity is antagonised by type 2 A protein phosphatase (PP2A) activity (Krahn et al., 2009), and silencing of tws, the regulatory B subunit of PP2A, results in Notch gain-of-function phenotype (Shiomi et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The fact that Spdo and Notch, two transmembrane proteins, colocalise with Baz in lateral clusters argues against a model according to which N-terminal oligomerisation domain of Baz could drive phase separation of Baz at this location.
source: The fact that Spdo and Notch, two transmembrane proteins, colocalise with Baz in lateral clusters (both on fixed and live specimens) argues against a model according to which N-terminal oligomerisation domain of Baz could drive phase separation of Baz (Liu et al., 2020) at this location.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and comparison to a proposed model.

claim: The nanoscopic clusters of Baz are reminiscent of the clusters serving as an AJ assembly landmark, by repositioning Cadherin-Catenin clusters at apico-lateral sites for assembly of SAJ.
source: The nanoscopic clusters of Baz are reminiscent of the clusters serving as an AJ assembly landmark, by repositioning Cadherin-Catenin clusters at apico-lateral sites for assembly of SAJ (McGill et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior published work.

claim: The Baz and Cadherin-Catenin clusters are shown to assemble independently and the number and size of Cadherin-Catenin clusters are decreased in the baz mutant.
source: The Baz and Cadherin-Catenin clusters are shown to assemble independently and the number and size of Cadherin-Catenin clusters are decreased in the baz mutant as reported here for Notch clusters.
evidence: This is based on comparison to prior published work and the current findings.

claim: Baz is required to position the cluster at the correct localisation along the pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: By analogy, it can be proposed that Notch/Spdo trans-interacting with Delta forms clusters independently of Baz clusters assembled through Baz oligomerisation, and that Baz is required to position the cluster at the correct localisation along the pIIa-pIIb interface.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on analogy to Cadherin-Catenin clusters.

claim: In vertebrates, Par3 functions as a receptor for exocyst, a protein complex of the secretory pathway required for the delivery of basolateral proteins to the plasma membrane.
source: In addition to organising membrane nanoscopic clusters of Cadherin and Catenin, in vertebrates, Par3 also functions as a receptor for exocyst, a protein complex of the secretory pathway required for the delivery of basolateral proteins to the plasma membrane (Ahmed and Macara, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Baz clusters are exclusively located at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: It is interesting to note that Baz clusters are exclusively located at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Analyses of NiGFP clone borders have revealed a preferential localisation of Notch at the pIIa-pIIb interface instead of being equally partitioned at the plasma membrane.
source: Analyses of NiGFP clone borders have revealed a preferential localisation of Notch at the pIIa-pIIb interface instead of being equally partitioned at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is based on clone border analysis experiments.

claim: Sec15, a component of the exocyst complex, regulates Notch and Spdo trafficking to regulate binary fate acquisition in the SO lineage.
source: Together with the fact that Sec15, a component of the exocyst complex, regulates Notch and Spdo trafficking to regulate binary fate acquisition in the SO lineage (Jafar-Nejad et al., 2005), our results place Baz as a potential regulator in the delivery of Notch/Spdo at specific sites along the pIIa-pIIb interface.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Baz is a potential regulator in the delivery of Notch/Spdo at specific sites along the pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: Together with the fact that Sec15, a component of the exocyst complex, regulates Notch and Spdo trafficking to regulate binary fate acquisition in the SO lineage (Jafar-Nejad et al., 2005), our results place Baz as a potential regulator in the delivery of Notch/Spdo at specific sites along the pIIa-pIIb interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and prior knowledge about exocyst function.

claim: Baz activity is required to define a threshold for Notch activation and Baz loss-of-function sensitises the ability of SOP daughters to signal.
source: We propose a model whereby Baz activity is required to define a threshold for Notch activation and Baz loss-of-function sensitises the ability of SOP daughters to signal.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The concomitant silencing of Delta and Baz, which individually induce a low rate of cell fate transformations, leads to a complete Notch loss-of-function phenotype.
source: In favour of this model, the concomitant silencing of Delta and Baz, which individually induce a low rate of cell fate transformations, leads to a complete Notch loss-of-function phenotype.
evidence: This is based on experimental results from double RNAi experiments.

claim: Silencing of Delta leads to a strong lateral inhibition defect, but the function of Dl during asymmetric cell division can be substituted almost completely by Ser.
source: Indeed, silencing of Delta leads to a strong lateral inhibition defect, but the function of Dl during asymmetric cell division can be substituted almost completely by Ser, explaining the tufting phenotype upon Delta silencing (Zeng et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In the Drosophila optic lobe, Notch, Serrate, and Canoe have been shown to form a complex.
source: It is worth noting that in the Drosophila optic lobe, Notch, Serrate, and Canoe have been shown to form a complex (Perez-Gomez et al., 2013), and Baz, by virtue of it regulating Canoe localisation (Choi et al., 2013), may regulate the distribution and/or activity of such a complex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Baz, by virtue of it regulating Canoe localisation, may regulate the distribution and/or activity of the Notch/Serrate/Canoe complex.
source: It is worth noting that in the Drosophila optic lobe, Notch, Serrate, and Canoe have been shown to form a complex (Perez-Gomez et al., 2013), and Baz, by virtue of it regulating Canoe localisation (Choi et al., 2013), may regulate the distribution and/or activity of such a complex.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from prior published work.

claim: Baz by regulating the size and number of clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface appears to be important for proper Notch signalling during SOP cytokinesis.
source: Whatever the mechanism of action, Baz by regulating the size and number of clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface appears to be important for proper Notch signalling during SOP cytokinesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The clusters present at the pIIa-pIIb interface are positive for Notch, Spdo, Baz, and Neur.
source: The clusters present at the pIIa-pIIb interface are positive for Notch, Spdo, Baz, and Neur.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Delta is detected along the pIIa-pIIb interface on fixed specimens.
source: While Delta is also detected along the pIIa-pIIb interface on fixed specimens (Bellec et al., 2021), DlGFP was reported to be barely detectable in living pupae unless Neur-mediated Delta endocytosis was blocked (Trylinski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: DlGFP was reported to be barely detectable in living pupae unless Neur-mediated Delta endocytosis was blocked.
source: While Delta is also detected along the pIIa-pIIb interface on fixed specimens (Bellec et al., 2021), DlGFP was reported to be barely detectable in living pupae unless Neur-mediated Delta endocytosis was blocked (Trylinski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Newly synthesised Delta reaches the plasma membrane and signals from there thus exhibiting a rapid turnover/endocytosis.
source: This led to the proposal that newly synthesised Delta reaches the plasma membrane and signals from there thus exhibiting a rapid turnover/endocytosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior published observations.

claim: The clusters are present on both sides of the pIIa-pIIb interface as a kind of snap button with Delta/Neur in the pIIb cell interacting in trans with Notch/Spdo in the pIIa cell.
source: An implication of these findings is that the clusters are present on both sides of the pIIa-pIIb interface as a kind of snap button with Delta/Neur in the pIIb cell interacting in trans with Notch/Spdo in the pIIa cell.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Based on the role of Numb in Notch/Spdo trafficking in the pIIb cell, the fact that Baz is enriched in the posterior pIIa cell at cytokinesis and the proposed antagonism between Numb and Baz, Baz is located primarily in clusters on the pIIa cell side.
source: Based on the role of Numb in Notch/Spdo trafficking in the pIIb cell, the fact that Baz is enriched in the posterior pIIa cell at cytokinesis and the proposed antagonism between Numb and Baz, we anticipate that Baz is located primarily in clusters on the pIIa cell side.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and proposed model.

claim: The time residence of Delta, Notch, and Baz in the cluster is very short (on the time scale of minutes).
source: As the time residence of Delta, Notch, and Baz in the cluster is very short (on the time scale of minutes), it implies that Delta can interact with Notch in trans, and be internalised in a Neur-dependent manner to promote the S2 cleavage of Notch in the minute time scale.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of cluster dynamics.

claim: Delta can interact with Notch in trans, and be internalised in a Neur-dependent manner to promote the S2 cleavage of Notch in the minute time scale.
source: As the time residence of Delta, Notch, and Baz in the cluster is very short (on the time scale of minutes), it implies that Delta can interact with Notch in trans, and be internalised in a Neur-dependent manner to promote the S2 cleavage of Notch in the minute time scale.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed dynamics and known mechanisms.

claim: Baz-mediated clustering might be a means to concentrate Notch/Spdo locally and increase its ability to interact with Delta.
source: We propose that Baz-mediated clustering might be a means to concentrate Notch/Spdo locally and increase its ability to interact with Delta.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Photobleaching and phototracking experiments during SOP cytokinesis reveal that among the two pools of Notch, the basolateral pool located basally to the midbody is the main contributor.
source: Photobleaching and phototracking experiments during SOP cytokinesis reveal that among the two pools of Notch, the basolateral pool located basally to the midbody is the main contributor (Trylinski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The composition of the presumptive signalling clusters are similar at the apical and basolateral pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: Our results, which show that the composition of the presumptive signalling clusters are similar at the apical and basolateral pIIa-pIIb interface, may indicate that NICD could be directly produced from both sites.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of cluster composition.

claim: NICD could be directly produced from both apical and basolateral sites at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: Our results, which show that the composition of the presumptive signalling clusters are similar at the apical and basolateral pIIa-pIIb interface, may indicate that NICD could be directly produced from both sites.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: The remodelling of cell polarity taking place during SOP cytokinesis could enable the formation of equally potent signalling clusters along the pIIa-pIIb interface, favouring private pIIa-pIIb cell-cell communication.
source: The remodelling of cell polarity taking place during SOP cytokinesis could thus enable the formation of equally potent signalling clusters along the pIIa-pIIb interface, favouring private pIIa-pIIb cell-cell communication.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The amounts and half-life of signalling clusters could account for the respective contributions of basal versus apical pools in producing NICD.
source: The amounts and half-life of such signalling clusters could account for the respective contributions of basal versus apical pools in producing NICD.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference.

claim: Upon a lack of Neur, Delta is bound to Notch in trans, and in the absence of Neur-mediated endocytosis of Delta that exerts pulling forces on Notch, the clusters are stabilised/not consumed.
source: Upon a lack of Neur, we anticipate that Delta is bound to Notch in trans. In the absence of Neur-mediated endocytosis of Delta that exerts pulling forces on Notch, the clusters are stabilised/not consumed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and known mechanisms.

claim: In the control situation, Numb is not detected in the Notch/Spdo clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface, suggesting that Notch and Spdo clusters at the interface are predominantly on the pIIa side.
source: In the control situation, Numb is not detected in the Notch/Spdo clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface, suggesting that Notch and Spdo clusters at the interface are predominantly on the pIIa side.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation that Numb does not colocalize with clusters.

claim: Loss of Numb that leads to recycling of Notch/Spdo towards the plasma membrane of the pIIb cell results in an increase in the number and intensity of Notch/Spdo/Baz clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: Loss of Numb that leads to recycling of Notch/Spdo towards the plasma membrane of the pIIb cell results in an increase in the number and intensity of Notch/Spdo/Baz clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and known function of Numb.

claim: Overexpression of Numb causes the disappearance of Notch/Spdo clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
source: By contrast, overexpression of Numb causes the disappearance of Notch/Spdo clusters at the pIIa-pIIb interface.
evidence: This is based on experimental results from Numb overexpression.

claim: By analogy with vertebrates, Numb, due to its ability to bind to Baz, is somehow competing with Baz for access to Notch/Sdpo, and therefore formation of Notch/Spdo/Baz signalling clusters.
source: By analogy with vertebrates, we anticipate that Numb, due to its ability to bind to Baz (Nishimura and Kaibuchi, 2007), is somehow competing with Baz for access to Notch/Sdpo, and therefore formation of Notch/Spdo/Baz signalling clusters.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on analogy to vertebrate studies and inference from the experimental results.

claim: Based on the fact that loss of Spdo leads to a stronger reduction in Baz/Notch cluster assembly, one prediction to be tested is that Baz interacts with Spdo/Notch.
source: Based on the fact that loss of Spdo leads to a stronger reduction in Baz/Notch cluster assembly, one prediction to be tested is that Baz interacts with Spdo/Notch.
evidence: This is a prediction based on inference from the experimental results.
